source: Trippas, Kellen, Singmann, Pennycook, Koehler, Fugelsang, Dube (2018) Characterizing belief bias in syllogistic reasoning: hierarchical Bayesian meta-analysis of ROC data
finding: The classic 2x2 table (Evans, Barston, Pollard 1983 Exp 1) as reproduced here: endorsement of 'valid' was .92 for valid-believable, .46 for valid-unbelievable, .92 for invalid-believable, .08 for invalid-unbelievable.
numbers: Interaction index = (.92-.92)-(.46-.08) = -.38. Mean endorsement .92 for believable vs .27 for unbelievable conclusions.
limits: Reproduced by the 2018 authors; the 1983 paper itself was not opened.
agent_relevance: Exact 2x2 baseline to test a model against: believable-invalid accepted as often as believable-valid.

source: Trippas, Kellen, Singmann, Pennycook, Koehler, Fugelsang, Dube (2018) Characterizing belief bias in syllogistic reasoning: hierarchical Bayesian meta-analysis of ROC data
finding: Across 22 confidence-rating studies the ROC curves are not systematically asymmetric, so the equal-variance signal detection model fits. Believability does not change discriminability on average.
numbers: 22 studies, N=993. Bayes factors for the equal-variance model 17.28 (believable) and 11.84 (unbelievable). Bayes factor 7.34 for no difference in da between believable and unbelievable. Participant, item and study heterogeneity all clearly above zero.
limits: Study 2 (simple syllogisms, near ceiling) had a slope above 1, so symmetry fails at extreme performance. Critics say confidence ratings may alter the decision.
agent_relevance: Most of the belief effect is a shift in the accept threshold, not worse logic. Measure acceptance bias and sensitivity separately.

source: Trippas, Kellen, Singmann, Pennycook, Koehler, Fugelsang, Dube (2018) Characterizing belief bias in syllogistic reasoning: hierarchical Bayesian meta-analysis of ROC data
finding: A new experiment (generalized area theorem) found symmetric ROCs without confidence ratings: picking the valid among M-1 invalid arguments is as hard as picking the invalid among M-1 valid ones.
numbers: Online sample, planned N=125. Correct choice probability when choosing invalid: .60, .43, .34 for M=2,3,4. When choosing valid: .64, .43, .38. Choice-focus effect -.03 [-.08, .02], Bayes factor 69.72 for the null.
limits: No believability manipulation in this experiment; abstract syllogisms only.
agent_relevance: Binary accept/reject rates can be analysed with hierarchical SDT without confidence ratings.

source: Trippas, Kellen, Singmann, Pennycook, Koehler, Fugelsang, Dube (2018) Characterizing belief bias in syllogistic reasoning: hierarchical Bayesian meta-analysis of ROC data
finding: Rival accounts: selective scrutiny (accept believable conclusions, check unbelievable ones), misinterpreted necessity (belief matters only when the conclusion is consistent with but not necessitated by the premises), mental models (search for counterexamples to unbelievable conclusions), transitive chain, Klauer et al 2000 MPT. Virtually all predict better discrimination for unbelievable conclusions.
numbers: Meta-analysis finds no average discrimination gap (Bayes factor 7.34 for the null).
limits: Authors say the result 'reiterates the challenge' to Dube 2010 and Klauer 2000 style theories. Individual differences and complexity may still produce accuracy effects.
agent_relevance: Do not build a step that assumes extra checking helps only for unwelcome conclusions.

source: Trippas, Kellen, Singmann, Pennycook, Koehler, Fugelsang, Dube (2018) Characterizing belief bias in syllogistic reasoning: hierarchical Bayesian meta-analysis of ROC data
finding: Pooling hides moderators. Trippas 2013 saw no belief effect on discriminability only for lower-ability participants, with higher-ability reasoners showing the usual accuracy gap. A pooled null means no average effect, not no effect in anyone.
numbers: Participant-, item- and study-level standard deviations had 95% credible intervals excluding 0.
limits: The ability claim is described second-hand from Trippas 2013.
agent_relevance: Report results per item type and per model size, not one pooled belief-bias number.

source: Trippas, Kellen, Singmann, Pennycook, Koehler, Fugelsang, Dube (2018) Characterizing belief bias in syllogistic reasoning: hierarchical Bayesian meta-analysis of ROC data
finding: In a conclusion-generation task the belief-discriminability result differed from evaluation tasks. Authors conclude evaluation and generation do not share the same processes, which hurts the mental-models claim that evaluation is implicit production.
numbers: Prior sensitivity check with wider Cauchy priors (scale 10 vs 4) gave essentially the same posteriors.
limits: Only a passage read; generation numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Checking a stated conclusion and producing one are different jobs; test the agent on each.

source: Trippas, Handley & Verde (2013) The SDT model of belief bias: complexity, time and cognitive ability mediate the effects of believability
finding: Believability affected accuracy on complex syllogisms but not simple ones. It also vanished under time pressure and for low-capacity participants.
numbers: No numbers read. Abstract level only via search and the 2018 paper.
limits: Original not opened.
agent_relevance: Smart models may show the accuracy side of belief bias more than weak ones; check by model size.

source: Trippas, Handley & Verde (2014) Fluency and belief bias in deductive reasoning: new indices for old effects
finding: Indices from raw endorsement rates break statistical assumptions and raise Type 1 error; SDT indices avoid this. Hard-to-read font made reasoning worse, not better.
numbers: N=76 undergraduates, 64 syllogisms each, 38 fluent vs 38 disfluent. Accuracy da .92 (Az 74%) fluent vs .51 (Az 64%) disfluent, F(1,74)=6.22, p=.015, eta2=.078, BF 3.30. Belief response bias unaffected, F<1. Overall belief bias t(75)=6.72; belief changed accuracy t(75)=2.81, BF 4.78.
limits: Contradicts Alter et al 2007 (disfluency helps) and Thompson et al 2013 (null). One lab, one manipulation, modest Bayes factor.
agent_relevance: Making the problem harder to process did not trigger deeper thinking; no reliable disfluency trick.

source: Trippas, Handley & Verde (2014) Fluency and belief bias: cognitive ability results
finding: Higher ability (short Raven) gave better accuracy and smaller belief response bias. The belief-accuracy effect appeared only in able reasoners who read the fluent font.
numbers: Median split. Ability on logic index F(1,72)=21.01, eta2=.23. Ability on belief response bias F(1,72)=9.59, p=.003, eta2=.12, BF 13.96. Ability x fluency on belief-accuracy effect F(1,72)=7.03, p=.01, eta2=.09; higher-ability fluent group t(15)=3.37, BF 11.34; lower-ability fluent group t(21)=0.28, BF 0.23.
limits: Median splits and cells of 15 to 22; short Raven only.
agent_relevance: Ability lowers response bias and raises sensitivity; report both when comparing models.

source: Trippas, Verde, Handley, Roser, McNair & Evans (2014) Modeling causal conditional reasoning data using SDT: caveats and new insights
finding: Syllogism ROCs are curvilinear as SDT expects (Dube 2011, Trippas 2013; but Klauer and Kellen 2010 disagree). For causal conditionals the expected pattern was violated, so SDT does not transfer automatically.
numbers: Four conditional forms discussed: modus ponens, modus tollens, affirmation of the consequent, denial of the antecedent. Syllogism results are cited, not newly run.
limits: Opinion article; a published comment exists (Frontiers 2014, article 402). Conditional-ROC numbers were not extracted.
agent_relevance: Check the ROC shape before trusting a d-prime on a new task type.

source: Dube, Rotello & Heit (2010) Assessing the belief bias effect with ROCs: it's a response bias effect
finding: ROCs from confidence ratings are curved, so raw accuracy differences between believable and unbelievable items can be artifacts of the linear model. Belief acts like a criterion shift.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Original not opened; known from search and the 2018 meta-analysis. Klauer and Kellen disputed it.
agent_relevance: Origin of the response-bias reading of belief bias.

source: Klauer & Kellen (2011) Assessing the belief bias effect with ROCs: reply to Dube, Rotello and Heit (2010)
finding: Disputed the curvilinear ROC claim and aggregation analysis (cited by Trippas 2014 as 'but see Klauer and Kellen').
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Original not opened. The 2018 meta-analysis largely favours symmetric curves.
agent_relevance: The response-bias reading is contested; use both descriptions.

source: Klauer, Musch & Naumer (2000) On belief bias in syllogistic reasoning (Psychological Review)
finding: Multinomial processing tree model supporting selective processing theory, in which beliefs affect reasoning itself.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Original not opened; described in Trippas 2014 and 2018.
agent_relevance: Main rival to the response-bias view: less scrutiny of believable conclusions.

source: Trippas, Thompson & Handley (2017) When fast logic meets slow belief: evidence for a parallel-processing model of belief bias
finding: Default-interventionist theory (fast belief answer pre-empts slow logic) is not supported. For simplest problems belief judgments were less accurate than validity judgments; for the most complex syllogisms belief interfered with validity judgments more than the reverse.
numbers: Exp 1 N=45 (modus ponens, modus tollens): accuracy conflict .68 vs no-conflict .92 (OR 2.88). Modus ponens: logic instructions .85 vs belief instructions .79. Conflict slowed responses 4786 vs 4503 ms (d=0.17). Exp 2 N=84 with three-term multiple-model syllogisms.
limits: Within-participant task mixing could cause response competition or task switching; authors argue it cannot explain the complexity pattern. RT effects less consistent than accuracy.
agent_relevance: Logic and belief are computed side by side; a separate logic pass should not depend on the first read.

source: Trippas, Thompson & Handley (2017): discussion of time pressure and capacity
finding: Usual story: a quick belief answer beats slow logic (Evans and Curtis-Holmes 2005). Parallel and conflict-detection work (De Neys) shows people notice the conflict but often fail to resolve it for logic. Capacity and analytic disposition moderate it.
numbers: Moderators cited: cognitive capacity (Evans et al 2010; Trippas 2013), analytic thinking disposition (Stanovich and West 1997; Trippas 2015).
limits: The time-pressure experiments were referenced, not opened.
agent_relevance: Treat detection and resolution as separate steps for the agent.

source: Evans & Curtis-Holmes (2005) Rapid responding increases belief bias: evidence for the dual-process theory of reasoning
finding: Time-limited responding increases belief bias, taken as support for dual-process theory.
numbers: No numbers read. Title and citation only.
limits: Not opened. Trippas 2013 reports belief-accuracy effects vanishing under time pressure, so the picture is mixed.
agent_relevance: Do not assume 'think faster' simply worsens belief bias; test it.

source: Pennycook, Cheyne, Koehler & Fugelsang (2013) Belief bias during reasoning among religious believers and skeptics
finding: More religiously skeptical participants made fewer errors on conflict syllogisms and spent longer on syllogisms. Longer response time went with less belief bias.
numbers: N=91. Religious belief correlated with conflict accuracy but not nonconflict accuracy, difference t(85)=2.73, p=.008. RT link held after controlling belief-rating RT (partial r=-.23, p=.028) and WordSum RT (r=-.22, p=.035).
limits: Correlational; eight syllogisms from Markovits and Nantel 1989, each shown twice; student sample. Ability was ruled out as mediator.
agent_relevance: Slowing down is part of the disposition that resists belief; a time budget per item is a symptom of override, not proof.

source: Markovits, Brisson, de Chantal & Thompson (2017) Interactions between inferential strategies and belief bias
finding: Reasoners using a statistical (likelihood) strategy are more swayed by conclusion belief than counterexample reasoners. Both groups seemed to detect the conflict (similar RT and feeling-of-rightness patterns).
numbers: Three studies, N=170, 189, 121 college students. Study 1 belief score (believable minus unbelievable acceptances out of 5): statistical M=2.47 (d=1.66), counterexample M=1.47 (d=1.04), F(1,168)=4.30 for the strategy difference. Statistical reasoners faster.
limits: Strategy classified from a pretest; order of tasks confounded with strategy use. French-speaking college sample.
agent_relevance: Counterexample search protects against belief; a scaffold step that builds counterexamples matches the protective strategy.

source: The effects of strength and activation level of belief on belief-biased reasoning (2024, Psychonomic Bulletin & Review)
finding: Belief bias scales with belief strength. Moderately believable conclusions still bias, but less than highly believable ones. Priming the category increased the bias.
numbers: Study 1 N=102 (Prolific). Acceptances out of 5 invalid syllogisms: prototypical M=2.65, nonprototypical M=2.25, neutral nonword M=1.43. Filler acceptance 96.6%.
limits: Online sample; invalid 'All A are B, X are B, so X are A' form. Authors cite Banks 2013 saying only strong beliefs bias.
agent_relevance: Belief is a graded dose; model confidence that the conclusion is true may predict its error.

source: Revlin, Leirer, Yopp & Yopp (1980) The belief-bias effect in formal reasoning: the influence of knowledge on logic
finding: Rival account: apparent belief bias partly reflects idiosyncratic encoding of the premises (e.g. converting 'All A are B'), not irrational switching. A rational-rule model predicted 80% of decisions.
numbers: Exp 1: model predicted 80% of decisions. Exp 2: 74.8% correct against 20% chance (observed 26.9% on guessed cases). Errors came from conflict between goals.
limits: Old, student sample, controversial premises; later work uses neutral content. Some counts were not fully extracted.
agent_relevance: Misreading the premises can look like belief bias; restating the premises first (S1) addresses it.

source: Lampinen, Dasgupta, Chan et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks (PNAS Nexus)
finding: Language models show the human belief-bias pattern on syllogism validity: strongly biased toward saying 'valid' for believable conclusions and somewhat toward 'invalid' for unbelievable ones.
numbers: Models: Chinchilla, PaLM 2 (M, L), Flan-PaLM 2, GPT-3.5. Item-level accuracy correlation humans vs models t(345)=4.98, p<.001. Paper cites Evans 1983 as 90% 'valid' for believable invalid conclusions.
limits: Short synthetic items; likelihood scoring with calibration; models are pre-reasoning-model era.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence the problem applies to LLMs; test with content-swapped matched items.

source: Lampinen et al. (2024): prompting, scale and instruction tuning
finding: In natural language inference a few examples or a short instruction cut content bias sharply. In syllogisms 5-shot prompting only slightly weakened content effects. Size and instruction tuning did not remove them.
numbers: Chinchilla 5-shot syllogisms: effects 'slightly weaker ... but remain robust'. Instruction-tuned models showed no consistent difference from base. Larger models more accurate but not necessarily weaker content effects.
limits: Likelihood-scored, small model families; no chain of thought or modern reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Prompt examples alone do not cure belief bias on validity judgments.

source: Lampinen et al. (2024): forced choice among conclusions
finding: When choosing among possible conclusions rather than judging one argument, Chinchilla had high accuracy and little bias, like the human forced-choice result of Trippas 2014.
numbers: Bias increased in the few-shot setting. Scoring method (calibrated vs raw likelihood) changed accuracy a lot.
limits: Appendix result; one model.
agent_relevance: Offer the agent a valid-versus-invalid pair instead of one argument.

source: Trippas, Verde & Handley (2014) Using forced choice to test belief bias in syllogistic reasoning
finding: In forced choice (one valid and one invalid argument shown together) there was initially no belief bias on accuracy. Showing one argument at a time, unbelievable conclusions were judged more accurately. Mediated by ability and analytic style.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Full text not opened (repository page returned HTML); abstract only.
agent_relevance: A comparison format removes much of the bias; a step could force pairwise comparison.

source: Trippas, Pennycook, Verde & Handley (2015) Better but still biased: analytic cognitive style and belief bias
finding: Analytic cognitive style, not ability alone, drives the link between ability and reasoning accuracy and response bias.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Only a search abstract; PDF fetch returned HTML.
agent_relevance: Disposition matters: a scaffold supplies the missing 'engage analytic mode' step.

source: Ozeki, Ando, Morishita, Abe, Mineshima & Okada (2024) Exploring reasoning biases in LLMs through syllogism: NeuBAROCO
finding: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 do worse on incongruent (belief-conflicting) syllogisms than congruent ones in English, and also show conversion and atmosphere errors.
numbers: NLI task English accuracy, congruent vs incongruent. GPT-4 in two settings: 76.24 vs 61.76 and 82.92 vs 67.23. GPT-3.5 in two settings: 56.19 vs 36.55 and 50.50 vs 39.92. Neutral class lowest. Japanese multiple-choice showed no clear congruence trend.
limits: Extracted table rows were hard to align with setting labels. Llama-2 and Swallow mostly failed to give valid answers.
agent_relevance: Belief-conflicting items cost strong models about 15 points; translating to formal logic first helped GPT-4.

source: Eisape, Tessler, Dasgupta, Sha, van Steenkiste & Linzen (2024) A systematic comparison of syllogistic reasoning in humans and language models
finding: Larger PaLM 2 models are more logical than smaller ones and than humans on abstract syllogisms, yet still show human-like errors (variable order, syllogistic fallacies). Only partial support that training on human text copies human errors.
numbers: Largest model's responses slightly more correlated with human responses than smaller ones, but it solves some syllogisms where humans fail.
limits: No belief manipulation: abstract content only, so this is general bias, not belief bias.
agent_relevance: Scale helps logic but does not erase human-like errors; test the contrast with and without content.
